concept.name: Scalping
concept.definition: An ultra-short-horizon trading style in which a trader opens and closes positions within seconds to minutes to capture very small price movements, often exploiting the bid-ask spread or momentary micro-imbalances in highly liquid instruments. It is the shortest-horizon form of day trading and relies on high trade frequency, tight risk limits, and low per-trade costs.
concept.intuition: Instead of trying to catch a big move, the scalper skims many tiny moves, accepting a few ticks of profit per trade and repeating this dozens or hundreds of times a day.
concept.mechanics: Positions are established and liquidated within minutes or seconds, using direct-access execution, level-2/order-book data, and strict stop discipline. Profit per trade is typically a fraction of a percent, so commissions, fees, and slippage must be minimized; small losses are cut immediately because a single large loss can erase dozens of wins.
concept.failure_modes: Transaction costs and slippage can exceed the small gross edge; during volatility spikes or thin liquidity, stops are jumped and small losses become large ones.
concept.misconceptions: That scalping is easy money because each trade is small and quick; in practice most retail scalpers lose after costs, and the SEC warns that day traders typically suffer severe financial losses. Scalping is also confused with the illegal practice of 'scalping' by advisers who tout a stock after secretly buying it.
concept.example: A trader buys 2,000 shares of a liquid large-cap stock at $50.01 and sells them seconds later at $50.04, capturing about $60 gross before fees, repeating the process many times per session.

citations.source: SEC, Day Trading: Your Dollars at Risk
